warmup.q: A team says: "We'll put GraphQL in front of our programs, so we get a graph database for free." With GraphQL, an app can ask a server for 50 payments, each with its account, in one request. In the simplest setup, the server fetches every field with a call of its own. How many calls reach the program that holds the accounts?
options: One: GraphQL joins the data inside the database
50: the code that fetches an account runs once per payment
None: GraphQL keeps a copy of every account it has seen
Two: one for each level of the request
warmup.why: GraphQL is a language for asking a server for data, not a database. The server runs a small function, a resolver, for each field of each object, so the account resolver runs once per payment: 50 calls, plus one for the list. That's the N+1 problem from the SQL track's lesson "SQL from the JVM: JDBC, pools, batching and migrations", one layer up. One call per level is what batching gets you, and it isn't the default.

sections.h: A fact in three parts: subject, predicate, object
sections.html:
The last lesson stored a graph as nodes and relationships, each with properties. Strip that down as far as it goes, and every fact becomes three short strings. M-0042 name "Northwind Bikes" says the shop M-0042 is called Northwind Bikes. C-7 owns M-0042 says the company C-7 owns it, and C-2 owns C-7 goes one level up. The first part is the subject, the second is the predicate (what's said about the subject), and the third is the object. When the object is a plain value, such as a name, the triple is a property. When it names another thing, the triple is an edge, a link in the graph. That's the whole data model of RDF, the Resource Description Framework, and a database that stores it is a triple store. The figure shows five triples as a table and as a graph.

Think of a card index where every card has exactly three boxes: who, what, and to whom or what. Here are four of the cards, written in Turtle, the easiest of RDF's text formats to read:

@prefix ex: <https://example.test/pay#> .

ex:M-0042  ex:name     "Northwind Bikes" .
ex:C-7     ex:owns     ex:M-0042 .
ex:C-2     ex:owns     ex:C-7 ;
           ex:country  "LU" .

Names in RDF are IRIs, web-style addresses used as global names, such as https://example.test/pay#C-7. The first line makes ex: a short way to write the start of each one, and a ; starts another triple about the same subject. Global names are RDF's real idea. Two collections of facts that both say https://example.test/pay#C-7 mean the same company, so you merge them by putting all the triples in one store. Merging two databases of tables needs both sides to agree on their tables and columns first.

SPARQL, RDF's query language, asks with triple patterns: triples with variables, names that start with ?, in some positions. "Who owns a company that owns M-0042, and in which country is it registered?" is:

SELECT ?owner ?country WHERE {
    ?owner  ex:owns     ?mid .
    ?mid    ex:owns     ex:M-0042 .
    ?owner  ex:country  ?country .
}

Each pattern matches triples, and a variable used twice must have the same value both times. So the first two patterns join on ?mid, and the third joins on ?owner. In card terms, you lay down three cards with blanks and ask for every way to fill the blanks so the cards agree. A SPARQL query is a join of one three-column table with itself, once per pattern. That's the picture for this lesson. A property path says "one or more steps" directly: ?c ex:owns+ ex:M-0042 finds every company above M-0042, at any depth. It's the loop from Recursive CTEs: trees and graphs in SQL, in one line.

Where does RDF stand in 2026? The Semantic Web it was built for, a web of pages that machines read as facts, never quite arrived, but the model lives on. Wikidata, the free knowledge base that Wikipedia draws on, publishes its facts as RDF and answers SPARQL. The schema.org labels that many web pages carry for search engines are often JSON-LD, which is RDF written as JSON, a common text format for nested data. And Amazon Neptune, Amazon's cloud graph database, answers SPARQL next to property graph queries.

The standards move slowly. RDF 1.2 Concepts and RDF 1.2 Semantics became Candidate Recommendations of the W3C, the group that writes web standards, on 7 April 2026: nearly final drafts. They add triple terms, a triple used as the object of another triple, so the store can say who reported an ownership and when. SPARQL 1.2 was still a Working Draft, an earlier stage, in mid-2026.

Triple patterns answer questions of a fixed shape. Next, we'll write a definition that walks any number of steps.

try.title: Turn a row into triples, and a question into patterns
steps: Take one row of the payments table: payment_id = 'pay-81723', account_id = 'A-1001', merchant_id = 'M-0042', amount_minor = 4250. Write it as triples, with ex:pay-81723 as the subject and one triple for each of the other columns.
Write the SPARQL triple patterns for "every shop account A-1001 paid, with the shop's name". Which variable joins which patterns?
Predict: if A-1001 paid M-0042 twice, how many rows come back, and what changes that to one?
try.expect:
ex:pay-81723  ex:account      ex:A-1001 .
ex:pay-81723  ex:merchant     ex:M-0042 .
ex:pay-81723  ex:amountMinor  4250 .

SELECT ?m ?name WHERE {
    ?p  ex:account   ex:A-1001 .
    ?p  ex:merchant  ?m .
    ?m  ex:name      ?name .
}

One row with three columns besides its key is three triples, which is why triple stores count billions of triples for millions of things. ?p joins the first two patterns, and ?m joins the second and third. Two payments to M-0042 give ?p two values, so two rows with the same shop. SELECT DISTINCT ?m ?name returns one, as DISTINCT does in SQL, where it drops repeated rows.

refs.title: W3C: RDF 1.2 Concepts and Abstract Data Model (Candidate Recommendation, 7 April 2026)

aside.title: Isn't a triple store only a table with three columns?
aside.html: Yes, and some are built exactly that way, on top of an ordinary database. What makes a triple store worth having is how it's indexed. It keeps the triples sorted several ways, such as by subject, by predicate and by object, so a pattern is one quick range read whichever of its three parts are fixed. A plain table with one index would answer some patterns fast and read everything for the rest.

sections.h: Rules that name themselves: Datalog, and the work a careless engine repeats
sections.html:
Triple patterns answer questions of a fixed shape. "Every company above M-0042, at any depth" needs a definition that refers to itself. Datalog is built for that. It's a database language from 1980s research, a cut-down form of the logic language Prolog. A program has facts, which are rows, and rules, which define new tables from old ones, the way a view (a saved query that reads like a table) does:

owns("C-7", "M-0042").    owns("C-2", "C-7").    owns("C-9", "C-7").

controls(X, Y) :- owns(X, Y).
controls(X, Z) :- controls(X, Y), owns(Y, Z).

Read :- as "if" and the comma as "and". Names with a capital letter, like X, are variables. The first rule says X controls Y if X owns Y. The second says X controls Z if X controls some Y and Y owns Z. That rule names controls on both sides, so it's recursive, and the shared variable Y is a join, like the shared ?mid in SPARQL. The program has no loop and no stop condition. The engine applies the rules round after round, until a round derives (works out) nothing new. That state is the fixpoint.

Back at the card index, the rules are pinned to the wall: "if one card says X owns Y and another says Y owns Z, write a card saying X controls Z". A clerk keeps applying them until a pass writes no new card.

The simplest engine, naive evaluation, applies every rule to everything known so far, every round. Count its work on a chain of 200 companies: C-1 owns C-2, which owns C-3, and so on to C-200. At the end there are 19,900 controls facts, one for each pair of companies on the chain. Naive evaluation needs 199 rounds, and round 150 joins again every fact that rounds 1 to 149 already found. It makes about 2.6 million derivations to keep 19,900. Double the chain, and the work grows about eight times; the Try it shows the curve. That's the clerk who rereads every card in the box on every pass.

Semi-naive evaluation fixes that with one observation: a new fact needs a new ingredient. If neither controls(X, Y) nor owns(Y, Z) changed since the last round, joining them again can only find old facts. So each round joins only the delta, the facts that were new in the round before. On the same chain that's 19,900 derivations, each fact exactly once, in the same 199 rounds. The clerk now reads only the cards written since the last pass. Where the picture breaks: a real clerk would notice a card they'd seen before, but an engine avoids repeated work only if it's built to.

You've met semi-naive evaluation already. In Recursive CTEs: trees and graphs in SQL, the working table of PostgreSQL, a free database program, held only the previous round's rows, and the recursive term read only those. That's this. The stepper runs it on four companies.

Datalog is a small corner of the database world and a busy tool outside it. Datomic is a database that Nubank, a Brazilian bank, made free in 2023. It answers queries in Datalog over datoms: a triple, plus the transaction, the group of changes, that wrote it and a flag that says added or removed. Soufflé turns Datalog into fast parallel C++ code that studies other programs without running them; its latest release is 2.5, from March 2025. GitHub's CodeQL finds security bugs in code with a language called QL, and its documentation says QL's meaning is based on Datalog, recursive rules included. Google's open-source Mangle adds aggregation (counting and adding up) to Datalog, as a library for the Go language.

Datalog and SPARQL both ask a store of facts directly. Next, we'll meet a language that asks a server instead.

try.title: Watch naive evaluation's work grow
steps: Read NaiveRoundsDemo.kt. It runs naive evaluation of the two controls rules on chains of 50, 100, 200 and 400 companies, and counts the rounds and the derivations.
Before you run it: how many facts does a chain of n companies have at the fixpoint? And if the derivations for 100 companies are about 320,000, what do you expect for 200?
Run it from the labs folder. The lab's semiNaive must bring the 200-company chain down to 19,900 derivations.

code.title: NaiveRoundsDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.model.l09.demo /** * Naive Datalog evaluation of * controls(X, Y) :- owns(X, Y). * controls(X, Z) :- controls(X, Y), owns(Y, Z). * on ownership chains of growing length. Every round joins ALL facts found so far. */ fun main() { println("companies facts rounds derivations") for (n in listOf(50, 100, 200, 400)) { // C-1 owns C-2 owns C-3 ... owns C-n val owns = (1 until n).map { "C-$it" to "C-${it + 1}" }.toSet() val next = owns.groupBy({ it.first }, { it.second }) var controls: Set<Pair<String, String>> = owns // the first rule copies owns var derivations = owns.size.toLong() var rounds = 0 while (true) { rounds++ val derived = HashSet<Pair<String, String>>() for ((x, y) in controls) for (z in next[y].orEmpty()) { derived += x to z; derivations++ } val grown = controls + derived if (grown.size == controls.size) break // a round that adds nothing: the fixpoint controls = grown } println("%9d %6d %6d %,11d".format(n, controls.size, rounds, derivations)) } }

try.expect:
companies  facts    rounds  derivations
       50    1225      49       39,249
      100    4950      99      323,499
      200   19900     199    2,626,999
      400   79800     399   21,173,999

The facts grow as n(n-1)/2, one for each pair of companies on the chain, and the rounds as n - 1, the longest path. The derivations grow about eight times for each doubling, roughly n³/3, because every round walks every fact found so far. At 200 companies, naive evaluation makes 132 derivations for each fact it keeps. Semi-naive makes exactly one.

refs.title: CodeQL: About the QL language (semantics based on Datalog)

sections.h: GraphQL: a way to ask a server for data, not a graph database
sections.html:
The third language in this lesson's title has "graph" in its name and isn't a database at all. An API is the set of requests that one program accepts from others: a phone app asks the company's server for data, and the server answers. GraphQL, which Facebook released as open source in 2015, is a query language for an API. A phone app or a web page sends one query that names the fields it wants, and the server answers with JSON in exactly that shape:

query {
  payments(merchant: "M-0042", last: 3) {
    id
    amountMinor
    account { iban customer { name } }
  }
}

The answer mirrors the query: a list of three payments, each with its account inside it, and each account with its customer's name. If two payments share an account, the account appears twice. GraphQL accepts that repetition on purpose, because the app gets something it can show on the screen without joining anything.

The server publishes a schema, a typed list of what can be asked, much like a Kotlin interface: type Payment { id: ID!, amountMinor: Int!, account: Account }, where ! means never null. An app can ask only for fields the schema declares, and follow only links the schema declares. There's no "every account within three steps" unless someone wrote a field for it, no recursion, and no filtering on any field you like. That's on purpose. Queries come from apps on strangers' phones, over the internet, so the server must be able to put a limit on what any query costs. Real servers also cap how deeply a query may nest and how much work it may ask for.

Behind the schema can be anything: PostgreSQL, DynamoDB (Amazon's key-value database), Neo4j, or three other programs. So GraphQL doesn't replace a data model. It lives in the API, the part of a system that the Encoding, APIs and workflows track covers, and it decides how many calls reach the stores below. That number is where it goes wrong, as the next section shows.

The specification, the document that defines GraphQL, changes slowly. The September 2025 edition is the first since October 2021. It added OneOf input objects, an input where exactly one field must be set, and schema coordinates, a standard way to name a field such as Payment.account. Sending parts of an answer early, with @defer and @stream, is still a proposal.

The schema decides what an app may ask. Next, we'll see what the server does to answer.

try.title: Predict an answer, and what the schema refuses
steps: The schema declares Query.payments(merchant, last), Payment { id, amountMinor, account }, Account { iban, customer } and Customer { name }. (An IBAN is a bank account number.) M-0042's three newest payments are pay-3 and pay-2 from account A-7, and pay-1 from account A-9.
Sketch the JSON answer to the query above. How many times does A-7's IBAN appear?
Does the server run { payments(merchant: "M-0042", last: 3) { account { payments { id } } } }? Decide before you read on.
try.expect:
{ "data": { "payments": [
    { "id": "pay-3", "amountMinor": ..., "account": { "iban": "<A-7's>", "customer": { "name": ... } } },
    { "id": "pay-2", "amountMinor": ..., "account": { "iban": "<A-7's>", "customer": { "name": ... } } },
    { "id": "pay-1", "amountMinor": ..., "account": { "iban": "<A-9's>", "customer": { "name": ... } } }
] } }

The answer has the query's shape and nothing else, and A-7's IBAN appears twice, once under each of its payments. The server refuses the second query with a validation error before it runs anything, because Account declares no payments field: an app can only follow links the schema offers. Add that field and the query becomes legal, and so does a query nested ten levels deep, which is why servers cap the depth.

sections.h: One call per field adds up to N+1 calls, and batching makes one call per level
sections.html:
The server builds that answer by walking down the query and calling a resolver, a function you write, for every field of every object. Query.payments runs once and returns 50 payments. Then Payment.account runs once per payment, each time asking the accounts program for one id: 50 calls. Then Account.customer runs once per account: 50 more. One query from the app became 101 calls behind the API.

This is the N+1 problem from the SQL track's lesson "SQL from the JVM: JDBC, pools, batching and migrations": one query for the list, then one for each item, moved up into the API. Every call is a round trip, a message there and an answer back. At about 2 ms a call, a fair figure for another program in the same data centre (a building full of servers), 101 calls is about 200 ms before any real work. The cost grows with the page size. GraphQL makes it worse in one way: the app chooses the query. A new screen can add a nested field and multiply your calls, with no change to the server at all.

Picture the card index again, kept in a back room. A careless clerk handed a list of 50 payments walks to the accounts drawer 50 times, once per payment. A sensible clerk reads the whole list first, writes down the 12 different account numbers on it, and makes one trip.

That sensible clerk is batching, the pattern that Facebook's DataLoader library made standard. A resolver doesn't fetch its one account at once. It hands the key to a loader and gets back a promise, a placeholder for an answer that comes later. When every resolver at that level has asked, the loader makes one call with all the different keys, accounts(ids). In SQL that's WHERE account_id = ANY(?), and in DynamoDB it's one BatchGetItem. Then the loader hands each resolver its record. Fifty payments that use 12 accounts cost one call for 12 ids. Do the same for customers, and the whole query costs 3 calls, one per level, however many payments the page shows. The loader also keeps each record for the rest of the request, so an account under 10 payments is fetched once.

A call per item is a cost that grows with every page. Batch by level. A test that counts the calls each query makes keeps the number from creeping back up.

DynamoDB single-table design and transactions passed on a warning from Alex DeBrie, who wrote a well-known book on DynamoDB, and it makes sense now. Single-table design stores everything one screen needs under one key, so one request fetches it all. A GraphQL server that resolves field by field throws that away, unless its resolvers know about the single table. Java and Kotlin frameworks, the ready-made foundations many servers are built on, put the batching where it belongs. Spring for GraphQL has @BatchMapping, and graphql-java has its own version of DataLoader, so you write one method that takes all the payments of a level and returns their accounts. The lab builds that by hand, so you can count the calls.

Every model in this track, from a key-value item to a triple, ends up as bytes in files on a disk. The next track opens up the part of a database that puts them there.

try.title: Count the calls one query makes
steps: Read ResolverCallsDemo.kt. It answers the payments query field by field, the naive way, for pages of 10, 50 and 200 payments. Every call to a program behind the API, a backend call, sleeps 2 ms, like a round trip to another program.
Predict the number of backend calls for each page size, and the time for 200 payments.
Run it from the labs folder. Then work out what a batched server would make for each page size.

code.title: ResolverCallsDemo.kt
code.html: package sfz.model.l09.demo /** * One GraphQL query, resolved field by field: * { payments(merchant: "M-0042", last: N) { id amountMinor account { iban customer { name } } } } * Each backend call sleeps 2 ms, a round trip to another service or a database on the same network. */ private var calls = 0 private fun roundTrip() { calls++; Thread.sleep(2) } private data class Pay(val id: Int, val accountId: Int) private data class Acct(val id: Int, val customerId: Int) // the three resolvers a naive server runs: Query.payments, Payment.account, Account.customer private fun payments(n: Int): List<Pay> { roundTrip(); return (1..n).map { Pay(it, it % 12) } } private fun account(id: Int): Acct { roundTrip(); return Acct(id, id % 5) } private fun customer(id: Int): String { roundTrip(); return "Customer $id" } fun main() { payments(1).forEach { account(it.accountId) } // warm up the JIT, untimed println("payments backend calls time") for (n in listOf(10, 50, 200)) { calls = 0 val start = System.nanoTime() val response = payments(n).map { p -> val a = account(p.accountId) // once per payment Triple(p.id, a.id, customer(a.customerId)) // once per account } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000 check(response.size == n) println("%8d %13d %d ms".format(n, calls, ms)) } }

try.expect:
payments  backend calls  time
      10             21  55 ms
      50            101  248 ms
     200            401  991 ms

The calls are exact: 1 + N + N. The times are from one run on a laptop, and come out at about 2.5 ms a call, because Thread.sleep(2) sleeps at least 2 ms; yours will be close. A page of 200 payments spends a second waiting on round trips. Batched, each page size makes 3 calls, about 8 ms.

opening:
Picture Northwind Bikes, a bike shop that takes card payments through the company. Before the company pays the shop, it must know who really owns it. The shop belongs to a company, C-7. Two other companies own C-7, and a fourth owns one of those. Each fact is tiny, "this owns that", and the question "who is at the top?" has to follow them up through any number of levels.

It's easy to think that any tool with "graph" in its name can answer that. One popular tool can't, and it hides a trap of its own.

Graph databases with Neo4j and Cypher stored nodes and relationships with properties, and drew patterns to walk them. In this lesson, we'll strip a graph down to facts of three parts, write two rules that find everyone at the top, and count the work a careless engine wastes. Then we'll meet GraphQL, the tool with "graph" in its name, and its trap. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a bike shop and the question of who is at the top of its owners. As triples, that's four facts and one property path; as Datalog, two rules run to a fixpoint by joining only what's new. GraphQL can't ask it unless the server offers a field that does.

On a site you use, open the developer tools (F12 in most browsers), choose the Network tab and type graphql in the filter box. If a request shows up, compare what it asked for with what came back.

That ends the Data models track. Next, the Storage engines track opens up the part of a database that turns these models into bytes on a disk, and asks when a write is really safe.

compare.title: Who controls M-0042: Datalog and a recursive CTE

a.label: Datalog
a.title: two rules and a query
a.html:
controls(X, Y) :- owns(X, Y).
controls(X, Z) :- controls(X, Y), owns(Y, Z).

?- controls(Who, "M-0042").

b.label: PostgreSQL WITH RECURSIVE
b.title: the same rules as SQL
b.html: WITH RECURSIVE controls(holder, company) AS ( SELECT holder, company FROM owns -- controls(X, Y) :- owns(X, Y). UNION SELECT c.holder, o.company -- controls(X, Z) :- FROM controls c -- controls(X, Y), JOIN owns o ON o.holder = c.company -- owns(Y, Z). ) SELECT holder FROM controls WHERE company = 'M-0042';

compare.note: Both say the same thing, and both run semi-naively: the CTE's recursive term reads only the working table, and UNION drops rows already found, so a cycle of ownership ends too. Datalog is shorter, because a rule is a join written with shared variables. An engine is also free to run it from either end. Given the fixed value in controls(Who, "M-0042"), it can rewrite the rules to start at M-0042 and walk upward (the magic-sets rewrite). The CTE as written works out every pair in the table and filters at the end, unless you start it from M-0042 yourself.

worked.title: Who is at the top of Northwind Bikes, asked three ways

steps.say: Start from the facts, as triples. Two companies own C-7, and C-7 owns the shop. C-1 sits one level higher.
steps.code:
ex:C-7  ex:owns  ex:M-0042 .
ex:C-2  ex:owns  ex:C-7 .
ex:C-9  ex:owns  ex:C-7 .
ex:C-1  ex:owns  ex:C-2 .

steps.say: SPARQL says "one or more owns steps" with a property path. The store follows ex:owns backward from M-0042 until it runs out.

Datalog says it with the two rules and a query, the line that starts with ?-. Semi-naive evaluation finds C-7 in round 0, C-2 and C-9 in round 1 and C-1 in round 2, then stops at the fixpoint in round 3, as the stepper showed.
steps.code:
controls(X, Y) :- owns(X, Y).
controls(X, Z) :- controls(X, Y), owns(Y, Z).
?- controls(C, "M-0042").
% C = "C-7" ; "C-2" ; "C-9" ; "C-1"

steps.say: GraphQL can't say it at all: there's no + and no recursion. The schema has to offer a field for it, and that field's resolver runs the recursion on the server, once, with one of the two forms above.

Count the calls. Say the schema offers owners on shops and companies, and the app nests it four levels deep. That costs a call for the shop, then one per company per level, and the app has to guess the depth. One field with the recursion on the server costs one call and needs no guess.
steps.code:
nested owners, 4 levels:  1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6 calls here, more with every level and every owner
controllers field:        1 call, any depth

lab.title: A triple store, a semi-naive evaluator and a batched resolver
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. No Docker is needed: this lab is plain Kotlin. 15 of the 17 tests fail with NotImplementedError; the two that pass check code you're given.

In TripleStore.kt, write match. For each stored triple, unify the pattern's subject, predicate and object with it, following the three rules in the comment above the function. To unify is to check that each part of the pattern fits the triple's value, and to give a variable its value the first time it's seen. query is given, and joins patterns with match. All six TripleStoreTest tests pass.

In Reachability.kt, naive is given. Write semiNaive: keep a delta, join only the delta with owns each round, count every pair you join as a derivation, and stop when a round adds nothing. The chain test expects 19,900 derivations on 200 companies, against naive's 2.6 million.

In Resolvers.kt, NaiveResolvers is given, and makes 100 calls for 50 payments (one payment's account no longer exists). Write BatchedResolvers.resolve with one call per level. The tests check that its answers match the naive ones, that it makes 3 calls, and which ids each call asked for.
hints: A private helper unify(term, value, bindings): Bindings? that returns null when they don't fit keeps match short. Run it for s, then p, then o, and keep the result if it isn't null.
Unify from left to right with the growing map of bindings, and Pattern("?x", "owns", "?x") works for free: by the time you reach the object, the subject has already given ?x its value.
In semiNaive, test each derived fact against everything known so far, not against the delta, or a cycle of ownership never ends.

payments.mapTo(LinkedHashSet()) { it.accountId } collects the different ids in the order they're first seen. Skip the call when the set is empty: the test for a shop with no payments expects exactly 1 call.

drill.title: Rules, a path and a batch from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. Write the two Datalog rules for controls over owns, and the SPARQL query for every company that controls ex:M-0042 at any depth. Then write one sentence on what semi-naive evaluation joins in a round, and one on what a batched resolver sends for each level.

answer.html:
controls(X, Y) :- owns(X, Y).
controls(X, Z) :- controls(X, Y), owns(Y, Z).

PREFIX ex: <https://example.test/pay#>
SELECT ?c WHERE { ?c ex:owns+ ex:M-0042 . }

Semi-naive: each round joins only the facts that were new in the previous round
(the delta) with owns, and stops when a round adds nothing (the fixpoint).
Batched resolver: one call per level of the query, carrying the distinct keys
that every resolver at that level asked for.

recap: RDF stores every fact as a triple (subject, predicate, object) with global names (IRIs), so two sets of facts merge by putting them in one store. A SPARQL query is a set of triple patterns, a join of one three-column table with itself, and a + property path walks any depth.
In November 2026, RDF 1.2, with triple terms, is a W3C Candidate Recommendation and SPARQL 1.2 a Working Draft. RDF lives on in Wikidata, JSON-LD and Amazon Neptune.

Datalog: facts are rows, rules are views, and a rule may name itself. Evaluation runs to a fixpoint. Semi-naive evaluation joins only the previous round's new facts, 19,900 derivations instead of 2.6 million on a 200-company chain, and it's what PostgreSQL's working table does.
Datalog lives on mostly inside tools: Datomic's queries, Soufflé's program analysis, GitHub's CodeQL and Google's Mangle.

GraphQL is a language for asking a server for data, over any store: the answer mirrors the query, apps can follow only the fields the schema declares, and there's no recursion. One resolver per field makes 1 + N + N calls; a loader that batches the different keys makes one call per level.

The limit: none of these three changes where the data sits or how fast one lookup is. A triple store still joins, Datalog still works out every fact it keeps, and GraphQL only passes questions on to the stores below it.

explain.prompt: The screen that shop owners use to see their payments got slow the week the mobile team added account { customer { name } } to its GraphQL query. Someone says: "It's still one GraphQL query, so it can't be the API." Explain what changed, and how you'd fix it.
explain.answer: It's one query from the phone, but not one call behind the API. A GraphQL server runs a resolver for every field of every object. For a page of 50 payments, the payments resolver runs once, then the new account resolver runs once per payment, and the customer resolver once per account, each a round trip to another program. So the page went from 1 call to 101, and at a couple of milliseconds a call that's about 200 ms more, growing with the page size. It's the N+1 problem from "SQL from the JVM: JDBC, pools, batching and migrations", one layer up. The fix is batching: a loader per type collects the account ids of all 50 payments and fetches them in one call with the different ids, then the same for customers. The query then costs 3 calls whatever the page size, and the loader keeps each record for the request, so a repeated account is fetched once. I'd also add a test that counts the backend calls per query, so the next nested field can't quietly do it again.

deeper.html:
Datalog gets interesting when rules say "not". Say a holding company, a company that exists to own others, is idle if it controls no shop:

company(X)  :- owns(X, _).
idle(X)     :- company(X), not controls_merchant(X).
controls_merchant(X) :- controls(X, M), merchant(M).

idle can be decided only once controls_merchant is complete, because a fact found later could make a "not" false. So engines split the program into strata, layers that each depend only on finished layers below, and run them in order. That's stratified negation, and a program whose recursion goes through a "not" has no such layers and is rejected. SQL has a similar rule: PostgreSQL refuses a recursive reference inside a subquery such as NOT EXISTS, or on the side of an outer join that may find no match.

The second trick is the magic-sets rewrite from the compare block. A query like controls(Who, "M-0042") only needs the facts on paths that end at M-0042. The engine rewrites the rules so that evaluation starts from the fixed value and walks backward, which turns "work out every pair, then filter" into "walk from the shop". You'd do the same by hand in a recursive CTE, by starting the anchor at M-0042.

RDF and property graphs differ most on links that carry properties. A property graph puts since: 2024-03-01 on the OWNS relationship. Classic RDF had to turn the link into a node of its own, with extra triples for the subject, the object and the date. RDF 1.2's triple terms are the standard's answer: a triple can now be the object of another triple. Stonebraker and Pavlo treat RDF as a subset of property graphs, and that's the gap they mean.

For the bigger picture, chapter 3 of Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, walks through triple stores, Datalog and GraphQL as query languages for graph-shaped data, and explains why GraphQL leaves recursion out on purpose.
